ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & UT Inspection | Detroit, MI
ut.description: Ultrasonic testing in Detroit: thickness surveys on piping, vessels and tanks and UT weld inspection on press frames, cranes and mill steel. Get a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Detroit, Michigan
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT provides ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection in Detroit for automotive plants, steel mills, the refinery corridor, power and utility boilers and structural fabricators. Technicians are mobilized to your site, take thickness readings or examine welds with angle-beam probes to a written procedure, and report results in a form your engineers and inspectors can act on. Send your scope through the Detroit UT quote request; we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic inspection is used in Detroit

Detroit's ultrasonic work follows its heavy industry. Automotive stamping and assembly plants have large press frames, crown and bed welds, crane runway girders and building steel that need weld examination as they age or after repair. The steel operations along the Detroit and Rouge rivers have roll shop equipment, mill housings, caster components, ladle cranes and piping that need both thickness surveys and weld checks. In southwest Detroit, refining and terminal piping, vessels and tanks require thickness data at condition monitoring locations, and the region's power plants and industrial boilers run thickness campaigns in outages.

Many Michigan plants also operate compressed air receivers, steam headers, hot water and chilled-water piping, and process vessels that sit under the state boiler and pressure vessel rules, which makes periodic thickness readings a regulatory matter as well as a maintenance one. Add the structural steel for the bridges and overpasses maintained by the Michigan Department of Transportation and the county road agencies, and ultrasonic testing becomes a routine tool in metro Detroit rather than a niche service.

What UT finds and what it misses

A short pulse of sound travels through steel and reflects from the back wall or from a flaw. Straight-beam readings convert the echo time into remaining wall, so a technician can measure corrosion loss on a pipe or vessel without cutting it. Angle-beam shear waves are aimed along weld fusion faces and root areas, where they reflect from lack of fusion, cracks, incomplete penetration and slag. That makes UT the working method for questions about weld volume and for thickness surveys, and it can estimate the height and length of a planar flaw when the geometry cooperates.

The method depends on good sound transmission. Heavy scale, flaking paint, rough weld caps and pitting scatter or interrupt the beam, so surfaces are cleaned first. Coarse-grained steel castings and some thick weld metal attenuate sound and limit usable range. Thin sections and tight geometries may need a different approach. A single point reading can miss a pit beside the probe, so corroded lines are scanned over a grid. UT does not detect all fine surface cracks as reliably as MT or PT, and it cannot identify the grade of steel.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Detroit UT work

Thickness measurement follows ASTM E797 and ASME Section V Article 23 (SE-797), and the data feed corrosion-rate and remaining-life calculations under API 510 for pressure vessels, API 570 for piping and API 653 for tanks. Weld examination follows ASME Section V Article 4, with acceptance from the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12, ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2, ASME B31.1, AWS D1.1 for structural welds and AWS D1.5 for bridges. Industrial and mill cranes and similar equipment are often covered by AWS D14.1, which the contract may call out for crane girder repairs.

In Michigan the Boiler Division of the Bureau of Construction Codes, part of the Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs, regulates boilers and pressure vessels, and the state adopts the National Board Inspection Code for repair and alteration. Michigan also runs a state plan through MIOSHA. Under API 510, 570 and 653 the owner-user authorized inspector remains responsible for the inspection program; Atlantis performs the UT and supplies the data, such as thickness at each condition monitoring location, so the inspector can calculate corrosion rate and remaining life. OSHA process safety management, 29 CFR 1910.119(j), requires mechanical integrity inspection at covered facilities.

How the examination is done

For thickness, the technician selects a dual-element probe for rough or corroded surfaces, calibrates on a step block of the same material, and checks against a known thickness at the start and periodically during the job. The A-scan is watched for lamination, doubling and pitting. Hot surfaces call for a high-temperature probe, suitable couplant and a correction for temperature, and the procedure states the maximum surface temperature for safe work. Readings are taken at the condition monitoring locations and on a grid where wall loss is suspected, and the grid is marked on the equipment so the next survey repeats the same points.

For welds, the technician prepares the scan surface, calibrates an angle-beam probe, typically 45, 60 or 70 degrees, on a reference block and builds a reference level or distance-amplitude curve from side-drilled holes. The weld and heat-affected zone are scanned from both sides where the geometry allows. Indications are located by position and depth, sized against the reference level, characterized and compared with the acceptance table. The report states when access limits the coverage.

Typical Detroit UT scopes at a glance

UT work by asset type in the Detroit area
AssetUT taskReference
Press frames, crown and bed weldsShear-wave examination of groove welds after repairAWS D1.1, ASME Section V Article 4
Crane runway girders and hoistsWeld and plate examinationAWS D14.1, AWS D1.1
Refinery and terminal pipingThickness at condition monitoring locationsAPI 570, ASTM E797
Vessels, receivers and heat exchanger shellsThickness grids on shell and headsAPI 510, ASME Section VIII
Boilers, steam headers and condensate linesWall thickness during outagesASME B31.1, state boiler rules
Highway and overpass steelWeld and plate examination per contractAWS D1.5

The scope depends on the damage mechanism the owner is tracking. Compressed air receivers and chilled-water lines tend to lose wall at low points where water collects, steam condensate lines at elbows and tees, refinery piping at injection points and dead legs. A crane girder repair calls for the new weld and a band of base metal beside it. Tell us the mechanism and the crew builds the grid around it.

Reading wall loss patterns in Detroit equipment

A thickness survey is only useful if it shows the pattern. Broad, even loss across a shell suggests general corrosion, a scatter of low readings suggests pitting, and a narrow band along the bottom of a horizontal line points to water settling out of the fluid. Detroit's older plants often have equipment that has been repaired several times, so an unexpectedly high reading may be a patch plate or a weld buildup and not original wall. The technician marks such locations and notes them on the sketch, because a corrosion rate calculated across a repair would mislead the inspector.

Production plants add another factor, which is access. Presses, conveyors and tooling often hide the piping and structure behind guards, and the work area may be shared with other trades. The plan identifies what must be opened, who lockouts the equipment and how long the area is available, so the survey is not cut short by a restart.

Who does the work

Level II technicians perform the examination and interpret results. They are qualified by their employer under a written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, and an ASNT NDT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Atlantis has no office in Detroit. Crews travel with calibrated equipment and the schedule is agreed against your shutdown or outage window. Procedures follow the code and edition in your contract.

What the UT report contains

  • Equipment or weld identification, location and drawing reference
  • Procedure and revision, code and edition, acceptance table applied
  • Instrument, probe, block, couplant and calibration checks
  • Technician name and qualification level
  • Thickness by grid or monitoring location with the minimum highlighted, or weld indications with position, length, depth and amplitude
  • Accept or reject, with sketches, thickness maps or photographs

Planning a UT job in Detroit

Automotive plants allow outside crews mostly in planned shutdowns, retooling periods and holiday weeks, and the production calendar, not the examination time, is the constraint. Press and crane work often needs lockout coordination and scaffolding from the plant. In winter, steel is cold and couplant gel stiffens, so winter couplant and warming are planned, and outdoor piping may need shelter. Refinery and steel sites require orientation, badging and permits, and elevated lines need access the owner arranges. Summer humidity can leave condensation on chilled-water lines that interferes with coupling. Share the equipment list, wall thicknesses, code and your outage dates early.

UT, MT or PT for your Detroit job

Choose UT for remaining wall or weld volume. Choose magnetic particle inspection in Detroit for surface and near-surface cracks in steel, especially forgings, hooks, tooling and structural welds. Choose liquid penetrant testing in Detroit for aluminum and stainless parts. Many jobs use two: UT for wall or volume, then MT or PT on the repair surface, which gives one consistent record for the repair file and a clear sequence for the crew. See the national UT service page, the ultrasonic thickness article and the Michigan inspection hub.

Training your own UT technicians in Detroit

If your plant wants in-house capability, Atlantis offers UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, with the UT simulator for practice. See the Detroit NDT training page for enrollment, and written practice development if you need a written practice.

faq.q: Do you perform ultrasonic testing in Detroit?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians are mobilized to Detroit plants and job sites for thickness surveys on vessels, piping and tanks and for shear-wave weld inspection, using a written procedure and calibrated equipment. Atlantis has no office in the city.

faq.q: What ultrasonic work do automotive plants need?
faq.a: Typical jobs are weld examination on press frames, crane runway girders and building steel, and thickness surveys on compressed air, steam, hot water and process piping. Work is scheduled around shutdowns and retooling windows.

faq.q: Which code do you follow for UT thickness measurement?
faq.a: Thickness work follows ASTM E797 and ASME Section V Article 23, with the data used under API 510, 570 or 653 where those apply. The owner's authorized inspector uses the readings for remaining life.

faq.q: Can UT take the place of radiography on a weld?
faq.a: Sometimes. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 have ultrasonic provisions, and ASME Section VIII permits it only under specific conditions. The owner, engineer and authorized inspector must approve the change before the job.

faq.q: Do you handle crane girders under AWS D14.1?
faq.a: Where the contract names AWS D14.1 for industrial and mill cranes, the UT procedure is written to that document and the acceptance criteria it references. We confirm the governing code and edition before mobilizing.

faq.q: Can you measure thickness on hot lines?
faq.a: Yes, within the limits of the procedure. High-temperature probes, suitable couplant and a temperature correction are specified, and the maximum safe surface temperature is agreed with your safety staff before anyone starts.

faq.q: How does a Detroit winter affect UT?
faq.a: Cold stiffens ordinary couplant and makes bare steel hard to scan outdoors. Winter couplant, warming and shelter are planned in advance, and the calibration is checked against the actual temperature range of the work.

faq.q: How are results presented?
faq.a: The report gives thickness by grid or monitoring location with the minimum highlighted, or weld indications by position and size, with accept or reject against the named criteria, sketches and maps, and reviewed by an ASNT Level III.

faq.q: How do I request a UT quote for Detroit?
faq.a: Send the equipment or weld list, wall thicknesses, governing code, location and your preferred outage window through the quote request. We reply within one business day to confirm scope and how the crew will be mobilized.

faq.q: What if equipment has been repaired and the readings look inconsistent?
faq.a: The technician marks patch plates, weld buildup and previous repairs on the sketch so that a high reading is not mistaken for original wall. Corrosion rates are then calculated from comparable points only, which keeps the remaining-life figure honest.

faq.q: Does UT work on welds in thick structural steel such as press frames?
faq.a: Yes. Press crown and bed welds are often thick, so the procedure selects probe angle and frequency for the section, builds the reference curve at the right depth and records any area where the geometry limits coverage. Thick welds may also be examined from both faces where access allows.

faq.q: Can you survey piping that is still in service?
faq.a: Yes, where the surface temperature and access allow it. Thickness readings are taken on live lines with the right probe and couplant, and the plan identifies any section that needs the system shut down, drained or locked out for safe access.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection in Detroit, MI | Michigan MPI
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection in Detroit and across Michigan for forgings, castings, tooling, cranes and steel welds. On-site MT to code. Request a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Detroit, Michigan
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT provides magnetic particle inspection in Detroit and across Michigan for steel weldments, forgings, castings, press and tooling structures, lifting equipment and refinery steel. Technicians are mobilized to your plant, forge shop or job site with portable yokes, particles and UV-A lights, examine ferromagnetic parts to a written procedure and report each indication against the acceptance criteria you specify. Use the Detroit MT quote request and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in Detroit

Detroit is where steel, forging and machining meet vehicles, and nearly every link in that chain gets magnetic particle work. Powertrain and chassis plants process crankshafts, camshafts, connecting rods, axle shafts, steering knuckles and gear blanks that are checked for cracks, seams and grinding burns. Forge shops and foundries around the metro area examine hot-forged and cast steel parts against customer drawings. The steel complexes along the Detroit and Rouge rivers, including the Zug Island blast furnaces and the Dearborn mill, rely on MT for roll necks, crane hooks, ladle hardware, couplings and structural welds in rolling and finishing lines.

Production benches inside the plants are usually owned and run by the manufacturer. The field work that people call on Atlantis for is different: press frames and die-set welds, robot fixture and tooling welds, building steel and crane runway repairs, lifting beams and hooks, rail car and truck frame repairs, and weld repairs after an outage. The refinery in southwest Detroit and the power and industrial boilers in the region add vessel, tank and piping attachment welds. People looking for magnetic particle inspection services in Michigan usually have one of these field jobs in mind, and the written procedure is tailored to it.

What MT finds and what it misses

Magnetic particle inspection works only on ferromagnetic material: carbon steel, low-alloy steel and most martensitic and precipitation-hardened steels. When a part is magnetized, a crack or seam that crosses the field leaks flux, and fine iron particles gather over it as a sharp line. The method finds surface-breaking cracks, laps, seams, quench cracks, grinding cracks and forging bursts, and flaws just below the surface. On forged and heat-treated steel it is the standard check for the thin, tight cracks that a visual look cannot see.

It cannot examine austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, magnesium, brass or most nickel alloys, which are not ferromagnetic; those parts need penetrant testing. A crack that runs parallel to the field does not show, so each area is examined in two directions about ninety degrees apart. MT sensitivity drops quickly with depth, and it does not size depth. Heavy paint, phosphate or oxide layers and rough surfaces weaken the indication. Some indications come from geometry, magnetic writing or changes in microstructure, and the technician must separate those non-relevant indications from true defects before anything is rejected.

Codes, specifications and Michigan requirements

Code work follows ASME Section V Article 7, with ASTM E1444 for the practice and ASTM E709 as the guide. Acceptance comes from the governing document: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2 for process piping, AWS D1.1 for structural welds, and AWS D1.5 for bridge welds on the state highway system. Forged steel is often examined to ASTM A275, steel castings use the surface acceptance criteria of ASTM A903 with reference photographs from ASTM E125, and automotive parts follow the customer drawing and quality system, which can be stricter than any consensus standard. The procedure names whichever document governs.

Michigan regulates boilers and pressure vessels through the Boiler Division of the Bureau of Construction Codes within the Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs, and the state adopts the National Board Inspection Code for repairs and alterations. MT after a repair weld is typically part of the record a state or insurance inspector reviews. Michigan also runs its own OSHA-approved state plan, administered by MIOSHA. Where API 510, 570 or 653 applies, the owner-user authorized inspector remains responsible for the inspection, and Atlantis reports the MT results to that inspector.

How the examination is done

The technician reviews the procedure, checks the yoke lifting power, cleans the area and sets up the lighting. Article 7 requires an AC yoke to lift at least 10 pounds at the maximum pole spacing used, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds. The yoke is placed across the weld or part, particles are applied dry or as a wet suspension from an aerosol or a squeeze bottle, the field is applied while the particles are on the surface, and the area is examined. The yoke is then turned about ninety degrees and the examination repeated. Prods are limited to places where a yoke will not reach and where arc burns on the surface are acceptable.

Fluorescent wet particles give the highest sensitivity on machined and fatigue-critical steel and are viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area; the procedure sets the UV-A intensity and the ambient white light limit. Visible contrast particles over white paint suit welds in lit areas. Field strength is verified with an indicator or a meter. After the examination, parts are demagnetized when residual fields would affect later welding, machining, bearings or sensors, and the residual field is measured.

Forgings, castings and tooling: what MT shows

Forged and cast steel fail in characteristic ways, and knowing them helps the technician read an indication. Forging laps and seams appear as straight or slightly curved lines that run with the grain flow. Quench and grinding cracks tend to form a network or run square to the grinding direction. Casting defects such as hot tears and cold shuts are rougher and more irregular, and shrinkage near gates and risers shows as clusters. Fatigue cracks in tooling and in-service parts start at a notch or a weld toe and grow in a clean line across the main stress direction. Each pattern points to a different cause, so the report records orientation and location and not just length.

Press and tooling steel brings its own issues. Die sets, tie rods, press crown welds and clamp fixtures see repeated loading, and cracks often start at repaired welds and sharp corners. Because the owner usually wants to know whether a part can run another shift, the procedure sets a clear accept or reject limit before the work starts and the technician marks the exact crack location on the part with a paint stick for the maintenance crew.

Common MT scopes in the Detroit area
ComponentTypical concernReference
Press frames, die sets, tie rodsFatigue cracks at welds and cornersAWS D1.1, owner specification
Forged shafts, hooks and axlesLaps, seams and service cracksASTM A275, ASTM E1444
Steel castingsHot tears, cold shuts and shrinkageASTM A903, ASTM E125
Mill rolls, ladle hardware, crane hooksSurface and fatigue cracksMill specification, crane standard
Refinery vessel and piping weldsSurface cracking after repairASME Section VIII Appendix 6, ASME B31.3

Quality system expectations in automotive and steel

Automotive and supplier plants work under customer quality requirements that sit on top of the technical standard: controlled work instructions, calibration records for equipment, retained records and documented corrective action. Our written procedures and reports are built to fit those habits. Every examination is recorded with the procedure revision, the equipment and the technician. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 for its own management systems. Steel plants add their own mill specifications and safety rules for entry to restricted areas, and the procedure and report format are agreed up front.

Who does the work

Level II technicians perform and interpret the work. They are qualified by their employer under a written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, while an ASNT NDT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Atlantis has no office in Detroit; crews travel to your site with their own equipment, and the schedule is agreed against your shutdown, tooling change or outage. Procedures are written to the code and edition on your purchase order or drawing.

What the MT report contains

  • Part, weld or tool identification, drawing reference and location
  • Procedure and revision, specification and acceptance table applied
  • Equipment: yoke or prod, current type, particle type and carrier, lifting-power check, UV-A and white light readings
  • Technician name and qualification level
  • Each indication: position, orientation, length, relevant or non-relevant, accept or reject, with photographs or sketches
  • Demagnetization and residual field record where required

Planning an MT job in Detroit

Detroit planning starts with the production calendar. Many automotive plants allow outside crews only during planned shutdowns, model changeovers and holiday weeks, so the examination has to fit a tight window and the area must be cleared of other trades. Winters along the Detroit River bring cold steel and lake-effect snow; wet carriers can freeze and contrast paint may not adhere, so a working-temperature limit is agreed or the part is warmed. Summer humidity condenses on cold forgings and tooling. Plants require orientation, lockout coordination and often a hot-work permit, and mills have restricted areas where a visit has to be scheduled. Share your list of parts or welds, materials and acceptance criteria early so the crew can arrive prepared.

MT, PT or UT for your Detroit job

Use MT for ferromagnetic steel when the concern is surface or near-surface cracking: forgings, shafts, hooks, structural welds and tooling. Use liquid penetrant testing in Detroit for aluminum castings, stainless parts and other non-magnetic material. Use ultrasonic testing in Detroit when you need wall thickness, weld volume or the depth of a crack. See the national MT service page, the MT guide, the Article 7 explainer and the Michigan inspection hub for related services.

Training your own MT technicians in Detroit

Plants and suppliers that want in-house magnetic particle capability can use MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training. The Detroit NDT training page explains enrollment, and NDT practice tests help candidates prepare. If your written practice needs updating, see written practice development.

faq.q: Do you provide magnetic particle inspection services in Michigan?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians are mobilized to Detroit and other Michigan plants, forge shops and job sites to examine ferromagnetic steel with yokes and wet or dry particles, using a written procedure to the specification or code in your contract.

faq.q: Can you inspect forgings and castings with MT?
faq.a: Yes, where the part is ferromagnetic. Forged steel is commonly examined to ASTM A275, steel castings to the surface acceptance criteria of ASTM A903, and automotive parts to the customer drawing. Atlantis uses portable equipment and works with the plant on setup.

faq.q: Which automotive components are examined by MT?
faq.a: Typical parts are crankshafts, axle shafts, steering knuckles, connecting rods and gear blanks in production, and press frames, die welds, robot fixtures and crane hooks in maintenance. Atlantis field work focuses on the maintenance and weld repair side.

faq.q: What cannot be examined with magnetic particles?
faq.a: Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, magnesium, copper alloys and most nickel alloys are not ferromagnetic, so MT cannot examine them. Those parts are examined by liquid penetrant testing, which finds cracks open to the surface.

faq.q: Do you use fluorescent particles under UV-A light?
faq.a: Yes, when the procedure calls for the extra sensitivity. The area is darkened, the UV-A intensity and white light are measured and recorded, and the technician allows time for eye adaptation before the examination starts.

faq.q: Is demagnetization included?
faq.a: Where residual magnetism could affect welding, machining, bearings or sensors, the part is demagnetized and the residual field is measured. Where it does not matter, the procedure records that demagnetization was not required.

faq.q: How do you handle winter conditions in Detroit?
faq.a: The procedure states a minimum working temperature for the carrier and the contrast paint. Cold parts are warmed or sheltered, and dry powder may be used where it is qualified. Outdoor jobs are scheduled to avoid snow and wind.

faq.q: What quality documents come with the job?
faq.a: The report records the procedure revision, equipment checks, technician level, indication locations and sizes, and accept or reject results. It can be formatted to fit a customer quality system, and it is reviewed by an ASNT Level III.

faq.q: How do I request an MT quote for Detroit?
faq.a: Send the part or weld list, materials, governing specification, location and your shutdown or outage window through the quote request. Expect a reply inside one business day, with questions about access, temperature and the acceptance table.

faq.q: Can you mark the exact crack location for the maintenance crew?
faq.a: Yes. Each relevant indication is located on the part or weld, marked with a paint stick or tape where the owner permits, photographed and entered on a sketch, so the repair crew can find it and the following re-examination checks the same spot.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing & Dye Penetrant | Detroit, MI
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing in Detroit for aluminum castings, machined parts, stainless and alloy welds. Visible and fluorescent PT in the field. Get a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Detroit, Michigan
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs liquid penetrant testing in Detroit and across Michigan, including dye penetrant inspection of aluminum castings, machined safety parts, stainless steel and alloy welds, and weld repairs on steel. Technicians are mobilized to your plant or job site, apply visible or fluorescent penetrant to a written procedure and report each indication. Request a quote through the Detroit PT quote request; we reply within one business day.

Liquid penetrant testing in Detroit: production lines and field repairs

Penetrant testing in Detroit falls into two kinds of work. The first is production inspection of castings and machined parts on penetrant lines inside plants, usually owned and operated by the manufacturer. The second is field PT on welds, repairs and non-magnetic components at plants, mills and job sites. Atlantis does the second: crews travel to the site with materials, lights and test panels, examine what the contract names and report the result.

The metro area's aluminum die castings, transmission and engine housings, brake and steering components, stainless exhaust and fuel system parts, and machined sealing faces are all candidates for penetrant testing because they are not magnetic or because MT cannot reach them. Field subjects include weld repairs on press frames and tooling, stainless and nickel alloy piping in utility and process plants, refinery fittings, valve bodies and weld overlay.

What PT finds and what it misses

PT finds flaws open to the surface: cracks, laps, cold shuts, shrinkage cracks and tears at the surface of castings, and porosity that breaks the surface. The penetrant enters the opening during the dwell time, the excess is removed, and the developer draws liquid back out as a visible stain or fluorescent glow. Because it depends on capillary action and not magnetism, it works on aluminum, magnesium, stainless steel, titanium, nickel alloys, ceramics and steel alike.

It is blind to anything that does not reach the surface. Smeared metal from machining, grinding or shot peening can close a crack, so such surfaces are etched or otherwise opened before testing. Oil, paint, flux, scale or water in a defect blocks the penetrant, and porous or very rough surfaces leave a background that hides fine indications. PT does not size depth, and it cannot find subsurface voids or inclusions inside a casting or weld.

Specifications and acceptance for Detroit PT work

For code work the procedure follows ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165, with ASTM E1417 as the process-control reference for fluorescent penetrant systems. ASTM E1417 expects routine system checks on a known-defect panel and control of UV-A intensity and ambient light; a supplier that runs a penetrant line should be able to show those records. Acceptance comes from the governing document: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 with Table 341.3.2, AWS D1.1 for structural welds, ASTM A903 for steel castings, or the customer drawing for automotive parts.

In Michigan, the Boiler Division of the Bureau of Construction Codes in the Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs regulates boilers and pressure vessels. PT on a boiler or vessel repair forms part of the repair documentation reviewed by the inspector under the National Board Inspection Code. MIOSHA administers Michigan's own OSHA-approved state plan. Where API 510, 570 or 653 governs, the owner's authorized inspector makes the decision about a defect, and Atlantis supplies the PT data.

Choosing the penetrant system

Most requests for liquid penetrant testing services come down to three choices, and a supplier should ask about all of them before quoting. The first is the penetrant type: fluorescent for higher sensitivity under UV-A light, or visible red dye for field work where the area cannot be darkened. The second is the removal method: water-washable, post-emulsifiable or solvent-removable. Solvent removal suits spot checks on welds and repairs, and post-emulsifiable systems suit production parts where fine cracks must not be washed out. The third is the sensitivity level and the governing document, because aerospace and many automotive part specifications state a sensitivity level, while pressure equipment follows Article 6 and the construction code.

Dip-tank and immersion penetrant lines are production processes where parts are dipped in penetrant, emulsifier or developer, with drain and dwell times controlled by the procedure. Atlantis works in the field with spray and wipe systems and does not run production dip lines. A user who searches for fluid immersion testing may be looking for that production process or for ultrasonic immersion tanks; if you need either, say so when you request a quote and we will tell you plainly what we can and cannot do.

How the examination is done

The technician checks the procedure and material lots, measures the part temperature and cleans the surface. Article 6 sets a standard range of 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the penetrant materials. Penetrant is applied by spray or brush and left for the dwell time. Excess is removed by the method the procedure names, developer is applied thinly, and the surface is examined at the development time under white light or UV-A light. Indications are classified, measured and compared with the acceptance table; doubtful indications are wiped, re-developed and examined again.

After inspection, penetrant and developer are removed so the surface is ready for welding, coating or service. On stainless steel and nickel alloys the consumables are chosen for low halogen and sulfur content and the lot numbers are recorded.

PT in a Michigan winter

A Detroit winter is the biggest planning problem for field PT. Outdoor steel below 40 degrees falls outside the standard range, so the part must be warmed and held in range, or the procedure must be qualified at the lower temperature with the comparator block method that Article 6 describes. A procedure written for summer work will not cover January along the Detroit River, and an auditor will check. Solvent cleaners evaporate slowly in the cold, developer dries poorly, and wind blows spray off the part. Plan an enclosure, a heater and extra drying time, or schedule the work in a heated bay.

Casting and machined-part defects penetrant testing shows

Aluminum and steel castings produce a recognizable family of surface defects. Shrinkage cracks and hot tears appear as jagged, branching lines near gates, risers and changes in section. Cold shuts show as smooth, curved lines where two metal streams failed to fuse. Surface porosity appears as scattered dots or short lines, and machining tears and laps show as short straight marks aligned with the tool path. Cracks in machined sealing faces and threaded features are the ones that matter in service, because they open under load and leak or propagate. A Detroit casting buyer usually needs the report to say which of these was found and where, so a rejected part can be traced back to its process.

In the field, PT on weld repairs is the standard way to prove a crack has been fully removed. After grinding out a crack in steel, the excavation is cleaned and tested before welding resumes; after the repair weld is complete and ground flush, it is tested again. The technician records both stages so the repair history is complete.

Surface preparation and contamination in Detroit plants

Plant surfaces rarely come ready for penetrant. Machined parts carry cutting oil and coolant residue that blocks the penetrant, castings may be shot blasted or impregnated, and aluminum can be anodized or conversion coated, which can hide fine cracks. Each condition has a cure written into the procedure: solvent or alkaline cleaning, drying, and in some cases light etching to remove smeared metal. Parts that have been impregnated or sealed must be tested before that step, because sealing closes the very defects PT is meant to find.

Steel castingsSurface discontinuitiesASTM A903

Who does the work

Level II technicians apply the penetrant system and interpret the results under a written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. An ASNT NDT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. Atlantis has no office in Detroit; crews travel to your site, and the schedule is set against your shutdown or outage window.

What the PT report contains

  • Part or weld identification, material and surface condition
  • Procedure and revision, specification and acceptance table
  • Penetrant type, removal method, developer form, lot numbers, dwell and development times, part temperature
  • Lighting conditions, and UV-A readings for fluorescent work
  • Technician name and level
  • Indications by location and size, accept or reject, with photographs or sketches

PT, MT or UT for your Detroit job

Choose PT for non-magnetic alloys and for aluminum castings. Choose magnetic particle inspection in Detroit for ferromagnetic steel, where it finds near-surface flaws as well. Choose ultrasonic testing in Detroit for wall thickness and weld volume. See the national PT service page, the Article 6 explainer and the Michigan inspection hub. A low-temperature or production PT procedure can be written through written practice and procedure support.

Training your own PT technicians in Detroit

Atlantis offers PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, with the PT simulator for practice. Enrollment details for the area are on the Detroit NDT training page.

faq.q: Do you offer liquid penetrant testing in Detroit?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians are mobilized to Detroit and other Michigan sites to carry out dye penetrant inspection on welds, castings and machined parts to a written procedure. Atlantis does field work and has no office in the city.

faq.q: Can you test aluminum castings with penetrant?
faq.a: Yes. Penetrant testing works on aluminum, magnesium, stainless steel and other non-magnetic materials, and it finds cracks, cold shuts and porosity that break the surface. Magnetic particle testing cannot examine those materials.

faq.q: What is the difference between fluorescent and visible penetrant?
faq.a: Fluorescent penetrant glows under UV-A light and is more sensitive, but needs a darkened area. Visible red dye can be examined in ordinary light, which suits most field jobs. The code or part specification decides which is required.

faq.q: Do you run production penetrant lines or dip tanks?
faq.a: No. Atlantis performs field PT with spray and wipe systems at your site. Production dip lines and ultrasonic immersion tanks are separate processes; tell us if you need one and we will explain what we can and cannot do.

faq.q: How does cold weather affect PT in Michigan?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 gives a standard range of 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Colder parts must be warmed and held in range, or the procedure qualified at the lower temperature, so winter jobs need heat, shelter and extra drying time.

faq.q: Which specification do you follow for fluorescent penetrant?
faq.a: Code work follows ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165. For fluorescent systems, ASTM E1417 is the process-control reference, covering system checks on a known-defect panel and control of UV-A intensity and ambient light.

faq.q: Who reviews boiler and pressure vessel repair documentation in Michigan?
faq.a: The Boiler Division of the Bureau of Construction Codes in the state Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs regulates boilers and vessels. The PT record, with procedure, technician and lot data, forms part of what the inspector reviews.

faq.q: What does the PT report include?
faq.a: It lists the part, procedure revision, penetrant lot numbers, dwell and development times, part temperature, lighting, technician, and each indication with location and size, plus accept or reject against the named criteria.

faq.q: How do I get a PT quote for Detroit?
faq.a: Send the parts or welds, materials, governing specification, location and dates through the quote request. We reply within one business day to confirm the scope and how the crew will be mobilized.

faq.q: Can anodized or impregnated aluminum parts be tested by PT?
faq.a: Anodizing and conversion coatings can hide fine cracks, and impregnation seals them. The procedure states how the surface is prepared, and sealed parts are tested before that step where possible. Any limit on sensitivity is recorded in the report.

faq.q: Do you test parts at the plant or take them away?
faq.a: PT is done at your plant or job site with portable materials. Parts are not taken to a laboratory unless you arrange that separately, so access, lighting and temperature at the point of work are agreed in advance.

faq.q: Will you test again after the repair is welded?
faq.a: Yes, when the scope says so. A common sequence is PT of the excavation after the crack is ground out, then PT of the finished repair weld, with both results recorded so the complete repair history appears in the report.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing in Detroit, MI | UT & Level III
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. Detroit options: UT as a volumetric alternative, Level III review of radiographs and RT theory training.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing in Detroit, Michigan: What Atlantis Offers
rt.html:
If you were searching for radiographic testing in Detroit, the direct answer is that Atlantis NDT does not perform radiographic testing in the United States. Industrial radiography is a licensed activity under Nuclear Regulatory Commission rules in 10 CFR Part 34 or the equivalent rules of an Agreement State, and it is not a service Atlantis provides here. This page explains what Atlantis does provide to Detroit customers who would otherwise reach for radiography.

UT as a volumetric alternative in Detroit

For many weld questions the real need is to see inside the weld, and ultrasonic examination can do that where the construction code and the owner permit it. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds. AWS D1.1 sets its own acceptance criteria for ultrasonic examination of groove welds on structural steel. ASME Section VIII allows ultrasonic examination in place of radiography only under specific conditions. Because substitution is never automatic, it is settled with the owner, the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector before the job begins, and the procedure is written to the governing code.

Technicians are mobilized to Detroit sites, and Atlantis has no office in the city. Read about ultrasonic testing in Detroit, or send your weld details and we will tell you whether UT is likely to satisfy your specification.

ASNT Level III radiography services without a radiation licence

Looking at radiographic evidence does not need a source license, because no exposure is made. Atlantis can review radiographs, film or digital images, and the technique sheets behind them, against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code. A second read on a disputed indication is a typical Detroit request, especially on castings, fabricated weldments and plant piping where a supplier and a buyer disagree about an image. Atlantis can also review an RT contractor's procedure and written practice before work starts, checking technique, sensitivity, image quality indicators and personnel qualification records.

  • Independent interpretation of radiographs and digital images against the acceptance criteria
  • Review of technique sheets, density, sensitivity and image quality indicators
  • Second opinion on borderline or disputed indications
  • Review of an RT contractor's procedure, qualification records and written practice

This work is led by ASNT NDT Level III personnel, including our founder Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis does not name or recommend radiography contractors, because the owner selects and contracts the licensed company directly.

Where the question arises in Detroit

Radiography questions in metro Detroit come up on cast and fabricated automotive tooling, steel mill weld repairs, refinery and utility piping, and pressure equipment shipped in from fabricators. The owner holds the code, and the acceptance decision stays with the owner or the inspector of record. Michigan boilers and pressure vessels are regulated by the Boiler Division within the state licensing department, so image records and procedures that are complete and consistent help at review. A second Level III reading can catch an interpretation problem early.

Training in radiography theory

Atlantis teaches a theory course for staff who want to read and judge radiographs: RT Level 2 course. It covers principles, image quality and interpretation following the SNT-TC-1A recommended practice. It is not radiation safety training and does not replace a radiographer license, which is a separate legal requirement. The Detroit NDT training page explains enrollment.

Other Atlantis inspection in Detroit

For cracks and wall loss, Atlantis supplies magnetic particle testing, liquid penetrant testing and ultrasonic thickness testing. See the Michigan inspection hub for the full range, and Level III consulting for procedure and report review.

faq.q: Is radiographic testing available from Atlantis in Detroit?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States because industrial radiography is a licensed activity. What Detroit customers can get is ultrasonic testing, an ASNT Level III second read of existing radiographs, and RT theory teaching.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on a Detroit weld?
faq.a: Sometimes, where the construction code and the owner allow it. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 contain ultrasonic provisions, and ASME Section VIII allows it only under specific conditions. Approval comes from the owner, engineer and authorized inspector.

faq.q: Can you give a second opinion on radiographs from another company?
faq.a: Yes. An ASNT Level III can review film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, and give an independent read on any disputed indication.

faq.q: Can you review a radiography contractor's written practice?
faq.a: Yes. A Level III review checks the procedure, the technique sheets and the written practice for personnel qualification against the code, so gaps are found before the contractor starts work.

faq.q: Do you teach radiographic interpretation?
faq.a: Atlantis teaches a Level 2 RT theory course under SNT-TC-1A. It is separate from radiation safety training and from radiographer licensing, which are handled by the licensed radiography employer.
